routes.label: Use the two triangle angle sums

question:
\[\angle 1 + \angle 2 = 180^\circ\] \[\angle 3 = \angle 4\] Find \(\angle 4\)

[Figure 1](figures/1997_AMC_8_Q12_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The left triangle has two known angles, so its angle sum determines \(\angle1\):
\[
\angle1=180^\circ-40^\circ-70^\circ=70^\circ.
\]
The given relation \(\angle1+\angle2=180^\circ\) then gives \(\angle2=110^\circ\).

In the right-hand triangle, the other two angles must sum to
\[
\angle3+\angle4=180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ.
\]
Since \(\angle3=\angle4\), each is half of \(70^\circ\). Thus \(\angle4=\boxed{35^\circ}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

reference.solution:
Method 1: Use the two triangle angle sums

The left triangle has two known angles, so its angle sum determines \(\angle1\):
\[
\angle1=180^\circ-40^\circ-70^\circ=70^\circ.
\]
The given relation \(\angle1+\angle2=180^\circ\) then gives \(\angle2=110^\circ\).

In the right-hand triangle, the other two angles must sum to
\[
\angle3+\angle4=180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ.
\]

edges.reason: Gemini confines its necessity argument to sexagesimal-format items. The actual criterion does not prescribe that format: decimal or whole-degree measures support angle addition and bisector calculations without minute/second conversion.

edges.reason: The target finds a scalar difference from 90 or 180 and distinguishes the two sum relations. It does not require the broader geometric angle-composition/bisector repertoire; Gemini conflates elementary subtraction of measures with that whole procedure.
edges.scope: Angle-composition and bisection experience supporting complements and supplements

edges.reason: Classification usefully organizes varied examples and helps check that the angle-sum rule is not confined to one type. The same straight-angle rearrangement establishes the rule for an unclassified triangle, so the useful role is preparation rather than necessity.
edges.scope: Organizing empirical triangle angle-sum checks across acute, right and obtuse examples
